scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if they're "AITA" (Am I the Asshole) for refusing to pump their girlfriend's tire. Let me break this down step by step.

First, I'll read through the scenario again to make sure I understand all the details. The girlfriend has a car that's been having maintenance issues, and she tends to hold the user accountable for fixing them. In the past, the user noticed a low tire, informed her, and later had to pump it for her. He even bought her a PSI gauge and taught her how to use it. But he made it clear that he doesn't know much about car repairs beyond basics like changing a tire or pumping air.

Now, another tire has a slow leak, and she's insisting that he check the pressure every morning and drive to the gas station to refill it. She claims she didn't know how to do it herself, didn't want to get dirty, and that it's a man's responsibility. The user is frustrated because he's already shown her how to do it and thinks she's playing the "Damsel in Distress" role. He's also done a lot of other things around the house, like cooking, cleaning, and paying most of the expenses, so he feels he's contributing enough without taking on this responsibility.

He offered to show her again how to use the pump, but she refused. Now he's determined not to help anymore. The question is, is he in the wrong for refusing?

I need to evaluate whether his refusal is morally acceptable. To do this, I'll consider a few factors: fairness, responsibility, communication, and mutual respect.

1. **Fairness**: The user has already taken the initiative to help her in the past, even going so far as to teach her how to use a PSI gauge. He's also handling other responsibilities like household chores and paying bills. It seems unfair for him to be the one consistently handling her car issues, especially when she's capable of doing it herself.

2. **Responsibility**: While it's kind to help out, there's a point where taking on too much responsibility can become enabling. If she's refusing to learn and keep relying on him, it might not be healthy for the relationship. He's trying to encourage her to take responsibility, which is a positive step.

3. **Communication**: He's communicated his boundaries clearly. He's explained that he doesn't feel it's fair to always handle her car issues and that she should learn to manage it herself. He's also offered help, but she's refused. This shows he's been reasonable in his approach.

4. **Mutual Respect**: He's respecting her by not enabling her dependence on him, and he's expecting the same respect in return. He's not holding her to stereotypical gender roles but is encouraging her to be self-sufficient, which is a positive value.

Considering all these points, it seems like his refusal is a reasonable response. He's already contributed by teaching her, and he's handling his share of responsibilities. Refusing to take on additional tasks that she's capable of handling doesn't seem morally wrong. It's about setting healthy boundaries in the relationship.

I should also think about whether there's any harm in his refusal. If he's not helping, does it cause her any significant harm? She's already shown that she can rely on strangers or family for help, so it doesn't seem like she's in immediate danger. Plus, he's made it clear that he's willing to help if she wants to learn, but she's choosing not to.

In conclusion, his action of refusing to pump her tire doesn't seem morally unacceptable. It's about maintaining balance and mutual responsibility in the relationship.
